title: Damayanti's act of truth
hookLine: five men with one face, and Damayanti finds the real one by the power of truth
carry: satya, truth, has a power of its own
last: A VRATA TURNS A STORY INTO A VOW.

cards: Five men in a row, every one with the same face. That's what Damayanti sees when she walks into her own swayamvara, garland in hand, ready to choose. Four of them are gods wearing the face of the man she loves.

One of them is the man. Last year we heard the whole story of Nala and Damayanti, from a golden swan to a long reunion. This time we stay with her: three days, three choices, and the first is made in a hall full of gods.

teach.b: Damayanti is the daughter of King Bhima of Vidarbha. She has chosen Nala in her heart before she ever sees him, because a swan carried his praises to her. Then four gods want her too: Indra, Agni, Varuna and Yama.
They even make Nala carry their offer, and she tells him plainly: she is his. On the day, the gods come wearing Nala's face. She can't tell them apart, so she doesn't guess.
She bows to the gods in her heart and speaks a chain of truths. In paraphrase: as I have never strayed from Nala in word or thought, by that truth, let the gods show him to me.
As I took this vow to honor him, by that truth, let them show themselves. And they do.

teach.h: NO SWEAT, NO BLINK, NO SHADOW
teach.b: The gods don't sweat. Their eyes don't blink. Their garlands stay fresh, no dust touches them, and they cast no shadow.
One figure has a shadow, dust and a wilting garland. That's the one she garlands, and the gods bless the couple. Here's the teaching.
In Hinduism, satya, truth, isn't only good manners. It has a power of its own. A truth lived all the way through can move even the gods, and Hindu stories come back to this again and again.

teach.h: SATYAM EVA JAYATE: TRUTH ALONE WINS
teach.b: The Mundaka Upanishad says it in three words, satyam eva jayate: truth alone wins. Those words sit under India's national emblem today.

teach.h: SATYA, TRUTH, HAS A POWER OF ITS OWN.
teach.b: And Gandhi named his whole nonviolent struggle satyagraha, holding fast to truth. Damayanti had no army in that hall. She had a promise she had never broken, and she said it out loud.

how: Hindus hear Damayanti's story in the Mahabharata's forest book, where the sage Brihadashva tells it to Yudhishthira; it is also retold in later poems, plays and dance across India.

o: a queen who won a husband in a contest of archery
a goddess who married the fire god Agni in a hall
a princess whose spoken truth made the gods show themselves

games.q: Damayanti's act of truth — tap the pairs.
p: truth, with a power of its own

s: Damayanti guessed which one was Nala
she asked the gods, by the truth of her faithfulness, to show themselves, and they did.
the gods cast no shadow and their garlands stayed fresh
and the one with a shadow, dust and a wilting garland was Nala.
satyagraha, Gandhi's word, means holding fast to truth
he built his nonviolent struggle on satya, truth.

games.q: you're Damayanti, garland in hand. five men stand before you with the same face. what do you do?
o: speak your truth: by my faithfulness, gods, show yourselves.
games.why: she speaks a chain of truths: as she has never strayed from Nala, by that truth let the gods show themselves. they do, and she garlands the man with a shadow.

practice: Many Hindus begin a puja with a sankalpa, a short spoken intention. Make one now: one true thing you mean to keep today, small enough to really keep. Say it once, quietly, then let your breath settle around it for a few breaths.
If you pray, you can offer it to God; if you don't, just hold it.

wordCard.voice: Damayanti. The princess of Vidarbha who spoke her truth to the gods, and found the man with a shadow.

orig.note: Sanskrit: the princess of Vidarbha, daughter of King Bhima, in the Mahabharata's story of Nala.

carryVoice: Your line: satya, truth, has a power of its own. Damayanti's moved the gods. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Mahabharata, Vana Parva, Nalopakhyana (the swan; the gods' offer carried by Nala; Damayanti's reply; the swayamvara; her appeal to the gods by the truth of her faithfulness and her vow; the marks of the gods; the gods' blessing)
